rubric: THE COMPUTER AND THE TRANSISTOR / CHAPTER 1

slides.title: The Computer and Levels of Abstraction
slides.main: We will travel the whole way: transistor, gates, processor, program.

captions: Start with physics: a transistor is a switch controlled by voltage
Transistors make gates, the first circuits that “decide”
Gates make memory, an adder, an ALU, and a whole processor
And the processor runs programs written in assembly

slides.title: Billions of transistors
slides.sub: Complexity too big to hold in your head
slides.main: Complexity is managed, not beaten: pick a level and forget the rest.

captions: One transistor is a simple switch, easy to understand
Thousands of transistors are already hard to keep in your head
Billions: only through levels of abstraction, not electron equations

slides.title: Abstraction
slides.sub: Leave out whatever does not matter now
slides.main: Each specialist gets their own level: the politician sees districts, the census sees towns.

captions: Details are not needed while the big picture is enough
The politician needs only districts: towns are not counted
The census bureau works at the lowest level and counts every town

frames.text: the whole country as one block

slides.title: Levels of abstraction
slides.main: The course covers the path from digital circuits to architecture.

captions: At the bottom are electrons and transistors: the realm of physicists and technologists
Analog circuits use continuous voltage, digital ones only two levels
Logic: gates build adders and memory, the core of our course
Architecture and microarchitecture bridge circuits to the OS and programs

frames.text:
voltage is
continuous
or two levels

slides.title: Architecture and microarchitecture
slides.main: One architecture, many microarchitectures of different price and speed.

captions: Architecture is a contract: the instructions and registers a programmer sees
A contract can be implemented in many ways: price, speed, and power differ
The same program runs on each of these processors

slides.title: Design discipline
slides.main: Digital circuits are simpler than analog ones, so systems are built from them.

captions: An analog signal takes any value, so a whole system is hard to analyze
Digital discipline allows only two levels, and everything gets simpler
Standard parts with tight tolerances can be swapped, like musket locks

frames.text: any part can be swapped for an identical one

slides.title: Three principles
slides.main: Divide into modules, define interfaces, reuse identical blocks.

captions: Hierarchy: a musket splits into modules, modules into parts, until it is clear
Modularity: each module has its own function and interface, no side effects
Regularity: identical parts are mass-produced and easily replaced

slides.title: Digital abstraction
slides.sub: Two voltage levels and the bit
slides.main: A bit is the amount of information in a variable with two states.

captions: A physical quantity varies continuously: wire voltage, gear position
A digital system picks values: high level is one, low level is zero
A variable with N states carries log₂ N bits: ten gear positions give 3.32 bits

slides.title: What abstraction gives us
slides.sub: Hardware need not be known, but helps
slides.main: Knowing neighboring levels helps write fast programs.

captions: A programmer sees a set of instructions and does not think about electrons
One program runs unchanged on different implementations
But knowing the processor lets you write faster code: optimize for it

slides.title: How the course works
slides.main: Slides, questions, and practice in every chapter: build the circuits yourself.

captions: First we see where zeros and ones come from and how they encode numbers and text
Then we build digital logic: you assemble every element yourself on the board
Next come registers, the ALU, memory, and the processor itself from blocks
And finally assembly programs and how fast systems are built
